name: Melanotan II

angle.text: Users inject melanotan II as a sunless tanning shortcut, aiming for darker skin with less sun exposure. It is an unapproved research peptide that also affects libido and appetite. Its tanning effect has been documented in small human studies, while claims of sunburn protection and equivalence with prescription afamelanotide rest largely on anecdote.

summary: Synthetic melanocortin agonist that darkens skin by cranking melanin production. Also hits arousal and appetite.
note: Unapproved, gray-market, FDA-flagged safety concerns. Not the same thing as prescription afamelanotide.
currentQuick:
Melanotan II (MT-II) is a synthetic cyclic peptide analogue of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone. It was developed in the 1980s at the University of Arizona as part of efforts to produce a sunless tanning agent, and it was also noticed to affect sexual arousal, which led to the later development of the related compound bremelanotide.
It has never been approved as a medicine in major jurisdictions, yet it is widely sold through gray-market vendors as an injectable or nasal-spray tanning product and is discussed heavily in looksmaxxing communities as a way to darken skin and reduce sunburn risk. Regulators such as the UK MHRA and Australia's TGA have issued warnings against its use, and it is distinct from the prescription drug afamelanotide.
How it works: MT-II is a non-selective agonist at several melanocortin receptors. Activation of MC1R on melanocytes shifts melanin synthesis toward eumelanin and darkens the skin, while activity at MC3R and MC4R in the brain is thought to account for effects on appetite, libido and spontaneous erections. Because it acts systemically rather than only on the skin, its effects are not limited to pigmentation.
Risks and caveats: Reported adverse effects include nausea, flushing, fatigue and unwanted erections, and there are case reports of priapism and renal infarction. Case reports and small series describe new or changing moles, including atypical naevi and several melanomas in users, although causation has not been established and users often had other risk factors. Products are unregulated, so purity, sterility and actual content are unverified. Evidence is limited to small early trials, case reports and anecdote; there are no long-term safety data.
deepLead:
Melanotan II (MT-II) is a synthetic cyclic peptide analogue of the hormone alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (alpha-MSH). It stimulates melanin production and was originally developed as a sunless tanning agent; it also increases sexual arousal in some users . It acts as a non-selective agonist at several melanocortin receptors, which is why its effects extend beyond skin pigmentation to appetite and erections .
Melanotan II has never been approved as a medicine. Development as a sexual-dysfunction drug was dropped in 2000 in favour of a related compound, bremelanotide, which was later approved by the US FDA for low sexual desire in women. Unlicensed melanotan II is nonetheless sold online and informally in some gyms and salons, and health agencies in several countries have issued warnings against its use since 2007 . It is a different compound from afamelanotide (originally called melanotan I), which is an approved prescription drug for a rare light-sensitivity disorder .
Small early human trials in the 1990s examined its tanning and erectogenic effects, and later literature consists mostly of case reports and reviews describing adverse events such as priapism, renal infarction, rhabdomyolysis and new or changing moles . Whether it affects melanoma risk is unresolved; reviews note that reported melanomas in users coincided with heavy ultraviolet exposure . It is discussed in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities as a way to obtain a tan with less sun exposure .

name: Afamelanotide

angle.text: Afamelanotide (melanotan I) is a prescription implant approved for a rare light-sensitivity disorder, and tanning communities discuss it as a supposedly gentler relative of melanotan II. The darkening is a side effect of its approved use. Claims about fewer moles or cosmetic use in healthy people are mostly anecdotal.

summary: MC1R agonist that boosts eumelanin and photoprotection.
note: Strong evidence only for its approved light-sensitivity condition — it is not a cosmetic tan drug.
currentQuick:
Afamelanotide, also called Melanotan I and sold as Scenesse, is a synthetic analogue of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone. It is delivered as a subcutaneous implant and is approved in the European Union and the United States for adults with erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP), a rare inherited disorder in which sunlight causes severe pain.
It is discussed in looksmaxxing communities because it darkens skin, and it is sometimes described as the approved counterpart of gray-market Melanotan II. The strong evidence applies only to its approved medical use; it is a prescription product for a specific disease and is not approved as a cosmetic tanning product.
How it works: Afamelanotide is a relatively selective agonist at the melanocortin-1 receptor on melanocytes. Stimulating MC1R increases production of eumelanin, the photoprotective brown-black pigment, and may also support DNA repair and antioxidant responses. In EPP the increased pigmentation and related effects allow patients to tolerate more light exposure before symptoms appear.
Risks and caveats: In clinical trials adverse events were generally mild, with headache, nausea and implant-site reactions most often reported; skin darkening and changes in existing moles are expected effects, so regular skin checks are advised. It is available only by prescription through specialist centres and is costly. Its safety data come from regulated clinical use and do not cover unregulated melanotan products.
deepLead:
Afamelanotide, sold as Scenesse and originally called melanotan I, is a synthetic analogue of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (alpha-MSH) that is delivered as a subcutaneous implant. It is approved to reduce phototoxicity in adults with erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP), a rare inherited condition in which light exposure causes severe pain .
It is a melanocortin 1 receptor (MC1R) agonist that increases melanin production and therefore darkens the skin . Because of this, it is often mentioned in looksmaxxing forums alongside the unlicensed peptide melanotan II, although the two are different molecules with different regulatory standing; afamelanotide is a prescription drug for a specific disease, while melanotan II has no approval .
Its best-supported evidence is from randomized, placebo-controlled trials in EPP, in which it increased pain-free time in light . Smaller or exploratory studies have examined it in vitiligo, acne, solar urticaria, Hailey-Hailey disease and other conditions . No trial has tested it as a cosmetic tanning product in healthy people on a large scale, and its approval does not extend to cosmetic use.

name: Dihydroxyacetone

angle.text: DHA is the active ingredient in self-tanning lotions, sprays and salon spray tans, used to get a bronzed look without sun exposure. The colour is a temporary surface stain rather than new pigment. Its cosmetic effect is well established; it is not a sunscreen, and application technique is a common forum topic.

summary: The active in every self-tanner: stains the outer skin layer brown. The only proven-safe tan in a bottle.
currentQuick:
Dihydroxyacetone (DHA) is a simple three-carbon sugar and the active ingredient in virtually all sunless tanning lotions, sprays and mousses. It is produced commercially by fermentation or chemical conversion of glycerol.
In looksmaxxing communities it is a common way to add a tan without UV exposure. It gives a temporary golden-brown colour that fades over several days as the outer skin sheds. It provides little or no sun protection, so it does not replace sunscreen.
How it works: DHA reacts with free amino groups of proteins and amino acids in the stratum corneum through the Maillard reaction, forming brown pigments called melanoidins. The colour is therefore a surface stain rather than a change in melanin production, and it fades as the keratinised cells exfoliate.
Risks and caveats: Topical use is considered low risk and DHA is a permitted colour additive for external application in the US. Reviews note it should not be ingested or inhaled, so spray-booth use needs eye, mouth and nose protection, and that long-term and inhalation safety data are limited. Skin irritation or contact allergy is uncommon. Reviews also note that users may overestimate their sun protection, since the colour does not shield against UV.
deepLead:
Dihydroxyacetone (DHA, also called glycerone) is a three-carbon sugar and the active ingredient in most sunless tanning lotions, sprays, mousses, wipes and salon spray tans . It darkens the outermost layer of the skin through a Maillard reaction with amino acids in keratin, producing brown pigments called melanoidins; the colour is a surface stain rather than new melanin .
The US FDA permits DHA as a colour additive for external application but not for the eyes, lips or mucous membranes, and recommends that users avoid ingesting or inhaling it; sunless tanners are regulated as cosmetics and cannot claim protection from ultraviolet radiation . Reviews note that more safety studies are warranted given how widespread its use is .
In looksmaxxing communities DHA self-tanner is discussed as a way to add colour without UV exposure, with threads on application mistakes, products and whether self-tanning is worthwhile compared to peptide tanning .

name: Canthaxanthin

chain: Carotenoid deposits in fat under skin
angle.text: Canthaxanthin was sold in oral tanning pills to give skin a golden-orange tint, using the same pigment that colours farmed salmon. The colour change is documented, but it is a pigment deposit rather than a true tan, and the pills have drawn regulatory and safety concerns.

summary: Carotenoid "tanning pill" that tints skin orange-brown at high doses.
note: Linked to crystal deposits in the retina. Unsafe strategy.
currentQuick:
Canthaxanthin is an orange-red carotenoid found in some bacteria, algae, fungi and animals such as flamingos and certain fish. It is used as a colour additive in animal feed, for example to tint salmon and egg yolks.
In the 1980s it was sold in high-dose oral "tanning pills" that deposited pigment in the skin to give an orange-brown tint. The colour was a pigment deposit rather than a melanin tan and offered no reliable UV protection, and the products were later restricted or warned against by regulators in several countries.
How it works: When taken at high doses over time the fat-soluble pigment accumulates in subcutaneous fat and skin, giving a diffuse orange coloration, a process distinct from melanin production. The same lipid-soluble pigment can also collect in other tissues, including the retina, where it forms the crystalline deposits seen in users.
Risks and caveats: High cumulative intake of tanning-pill doses has been associated with canthaxanthin crystalline retinopathy, in which glittering yellow crystals appear around the macula; visual function is often preserved but deposits can persist for years. Other reported problems include gastrointestinal upset, hives and rare liver or blood effects. In the US the FDA has not approved it for tanning, so use for that purpose is unapproved.
deepLead:
Canthaxanthin is an orange-red keto-carotenoid pigment (C40H52O2) found in some mushrooms, algae, bacteria and crustaceans, and used as a food and feed colourant, for example to colour farmed salmon, trout and egg yolks . When swallowed in large amounts, it deposits in fat beneath the skin and gives a golden-orange tint, which is why it was sold in oral 'tanning pills' .
This colour is not melanin-based. High-dose tanning-pill use has been associated with canthaxanthin retinopathy, in which yellow crystalline deposits appear in the retina, and with reports of urticaria and liver injury, according to the US FDA and the American Academy of Dermatology as summarised on Wikipedia . The FDA has no tanning pills approved for sale in the US and has sent warning letters to firms marketing canthaxanthin pills as 'adulterated cosmetics' with an unsafe colour additive .
Controlled human studies from the 1970s and 1980s combined canthaxanthin with beta-carotene in photodermatoses and as an oral skin-colouring agent . It is discussed on T Nation and other forums from the early 2000s as a possible pill for a tan-like colour .

name: Beta-carotene

angle.text: Looksmaxxing forums discuss beta-carotene, from food or supplements, as a way to give skin a warmer, golden colour. Studies have measured small skin colour shifts from high carotenoid intake, and some people report an orange cast. Whether the result reads as attractive is a matter of debate among users.

summary: Gives skin a warmer, golden tone with sustained daily intake.
currentQuick:
Beta-carotene is a yellow-orange carotenoid pigment found in carrots, sweet potatoes and leafy greens, and it is a dietary precursor of vitamin A. It is sold as a supplement and used in some sunless-tan and skin-glow products.
In appearance circles it is used to add a warm, golden-yellow tint to the skin. Small human trials suggest that sustained intake raises skin yellowness and that observers can rate the resulting faces as healthier or more attractive, mainly in lightly pigmented skin.
How it works: After absorption with dietary fat, beta-carotene circulates in lipoproteins and is deposited in the skin, particularly in the stratum corneum and subcutaneous fat. The deposited pigment adds a yellow-orange hue to the skin's reflectance. Some is converted to retinol in the body, and it also has antioxidant activity in tissues.
Risks and caveats: Very high intake can cause carotenemia, a harmless but visible orange discolouration that fades after intake is reduced. Large randomized trials in smokers and people exposed to asbestos found that high-dose beta-carotene supplements increased lung cancer risk, and high-dose supplements are therefore generally advised against for these groups. Studies report the cosmetic effect as modest and variable, and weaker in darker, sun-exposed skin.
deepLead:
Beta-carotene is a yellow-orange carotenoid pigment found in carrots, sweet potatoes and leafy greens, and is a dietary precursor of vitamin A . It is sold as a supplement and is discussed in looksmaxxing communities as a way to give skin a warmer, golden tone through sustained oral intake .
The pigment is fat-soluble and accumulates in serum and skin, and research has examined this accumulation  including in African skin . Community members report mixed outcomes, from a golden tone to no visible change or an orange cast .
Large randomized trials of high-dose beta-carotene supplements in smokers and asbestos-exposed workers found no reduction in lung cancer and, in the CARET trial, a relative risk of 1.28 in the combined beta-carotene and retinol group . This finding is the main safety concern raised by researchers and is also discussed by looksmax.org users asking about smoking .

name: Lycopene

angle.text: Lycopene, from cooked tomatoes or supplements, is mentioned in skin and tan communities as a mild internal photoprotectant and a source of a warm, reddish tint. Small trials have looked at UV-induced redness; evidence for visible tanning or lasting appearance changes is limited.

summary: Tomato carotenoid with antioxidant and mild photoprotective effects.
currentQuick:
Lycopene is the red carotenoid pigment that gives tomatoes, watermelon and pink grapefruit their colour. It is consumed through food, especially cooked tomato products, and as a supplement.
In skincare it is promoted as an internal photoprotective antioxidant. Intervention trials suggest small reductions in UV-induced redness and some markers of photodamage, but the reported effects are modest and lycopene is not a substitute for sunscreen.
How it works: Lycopene is a highly lipophilic molecule that accumulates in skin and is an efficient quencher of singlet oxygen and other reactive oxygen species. By limiting UV-driven oxidative damage and downstream inflammatory and matrix-degrading signals, it is thought to blunt part of the sunburn response. Absorption improves when it is eaten with fat and after heat processing.
Risks and caveats: Dietary and supplement doses are generally well tolerated. Very high intake can cause lycopenemia, a harmless orange tint to the skin that resolves after reducing intake. Many trials are small and often use tomato paste or industry-supplied extracts, which limits the strength of the findings.
deepLead:
Lycopene is a bright red carotenoid hydrocarbon found in tomatoes, watermelon, pink grapefruit, red guava and some other red fruits and vegetables. Unlike beta-carotene, it has no vitamin A activity, and it is also used as a food colour (E160d) . It is taken through food, especially cooked tomato products eaten with fat, and as a supplement .
In skincare and appearance contexts, lycopene is promoted as an internal antioxidant that may reduce UV-related skin damage and give a warmer tone. A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of 21 intervention trials found that tomato and lycopene supplementation was associated with reductions in erythema-related measures, MMP-1, ICAM-1 and skin pigmentation, and increases in minimal erythema dose, skin thickness and density . Regulators have taken a more cautious view: the European Food Safety Authority concluded there was insufficient evidence for antioxidant effects in humans, including in skin .
High intake can cause lycopenemia, an orange skin discolouration that is expected to fade after intake is reduced . Lycopene is non-toxic in dietary amounts, though intolerance, interactions with blood-pressure drugs and anticoagulants have been noted .

name: Astaxanthin

angle.text: Astaxanthin is taken as a supplement for skin glow, anti-aging and a slightly warmer tone. Some small trials have measured skin moisture, elasticity and UV redness. Its role in estrogen control on TRT is a forum claim that rests on anecdote.

summary: Carotenoid studied for UV damage, skin moisture, and elasticity.
currentQuick:
Astaxanthin is a red-pink xanthophyll carotenoid made by microalgae such as Haematococcus pluvialis and responsible for the colour of salmon, shrimp and flamingos. It is sold as a dietary supplement, typically derived from algae.
In looksmaxxing and skincare it is used for skin hydration, elasticity and defence against UV damage. Systematic reviews find modest improvements in moisture and elasticity in small trials, with less consistent effects on wrinkles.
How it works: Astaxanthin is a potent lipid-soluble antioxidant that spans cell membranes and quenches reactive oxygen species, and in cell studies it dampens UV-induced inflammatory signalling and collagen-degrading enzymes. Whether these effects translate into meaningful clinical change depends on the trials, which are mostly short.
Risks and caveats: Supplements are generally well tolerated at studied doses, with occasional mild gastrointestinal effects and, at high intake, a reddish skin tint. Safety in pregnancy and long-term use is not well established. Most trials are small, many are industry-funded, and several enrolled mainly healthy Japanese women, limiting how far results generalise.
deepLead:
Astaxanthin is a red keto-carotenoid pigment produced by the freshwater microalga Haematococcus pluvialis, the yeast Xanthophyllomyces dendrorhous and the bacterium Paracoccus carotinifaciens, and it is responsible for the pink-red colour of salmon, shrimp, krill and flamingos . It is sold as a dietary supplement and, in synthetic form, is widely used as a feed colourant in aquaculture .
In appearance and skincare communities it is taken for skin hydration, elasticity and protection from UV-induced skin deterioration . A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials found that oral astaxanthin significantly improved moisture and elasticity compared with placebo but did not significantly reduce wrinkle depth . Trials are mostly small and short.
It is regarded as generally recognized as safe in the United States for algae, synthetic and bacterial sources, and the EFSA set an acceptable daily intake of 0.2 mg per kg body weight in 2019 . On T Nation it is mentioned mainly as an anti-inflammatory supplement .

name: Polypodium leucotomos

angle.text: Users take Polypodium leucotomos extract as an 'internal sunscreen' alongside tanning, or to limit sun-driven dark spots and aging. Small trials have studied reduced sunburn reactions and some pigmentation conditions such as melasma. It is not a replacement for topical sunscreen in the studies.

summary: Fern extract that blunts some UV-induced skin reactions.
currentQuick:
Polypodium leucotomos is a tropical fern native to Central and South America whose leaf extract is sold as an oral supplement, for example under the Fernblock and Heliocare names. It has a long history in traditional medicine and has been studied in dermatology for UV-related skin reactions.
In the appearance space it is used as an "internal sunscreen" adjunct to reduce sunburn, photoaging and pigmentation. Clinical studies suggest modest benefit, and it is not regarded as a substitute for sunscreen.
How it works: The extract is rich in phenolic compounds with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity. In studies it reduces UV-induced DNA damage and inflammatory mediators, limits generation of reactive oxygen species, and may support Langerhans cell function in skin. It does not absorb UV like a sunscreen filter.
Risks and caveats: Oral extract is generally well tolerated, with occasional mild gastrointestinal upset, headache or itching; serious adverse effects have not been reported in published reviews. Evidence comes from small trials with varied formulations, so supplements that do not specify the studied extract may not be equivalent.
deepLead:
Polypodium leucotomos is the older botanical name for Phlebodium aureum, an epiphytic fern native to tropical and subtropical regions of the Americas. Extract from its leaves is sold as an oral supplement, including under the Heliocare name, and has been studied in dermatology as an 'internal' or systemic photoprotective agent .
Decoctions were used in Central American folk medicine, and modern research has examined the extract for conditions including melasma, vitiligo, psoriasis, polymorphous light eruption, atopic dermatitis, postinflammatory hyperpigmentation, photoaging and skin cancer . A 2025 systematic review of oral photoprotective supplements found the greatest evidence among polyphenols, carotenoids and Polypodium leucotomos .
Reviews also note limits: few trials support supplements as monotherapy or as an alternative to sunscreen, and trials are small with varied formulations . In looksmaxxing forums it appears as a supplement to combine with tanning peptides and to reduce the sun exposure needed for a tan .

name: Glutathione

angle.text: Glutathione, oral or injected, is promoted for skin lightening and a brighter complexion, mainly in parts of Asia, and it is also taken as a general antioxidant by lifters. Small trials report modest lightening in some participants, though results are inconsistent and injectable use is largely unregulated.

summary: Antioxidant heavily marketed for skin lightening; visible results are inconsistent.
currentQuick:
Glutathione is a tripeptide made of glutamate, cysteine and glycine and is the main small-molecule antioxidant inside most cells. It is available as oral, sublingual, topical and intravenous products.
It is widely marketed, particularly in parts of Asia, for skin lightening, and it is discussed in looksmaxxing forums for the same purpose. Controlled evidence of visible whitening is limited and inconsistent, and professional bodies have warned against intravenous use for this purpose.
How it works: Proposed lightening mechanisms include inhibition of tyrosinase, the key melanin-producing enzyme, and a shift from darker eumelanin toward lighter pheomelanin through cysteine availability. Oral glutathione is poorly absorbed and largely broken down in the gut, so it is unclear how much reaches skin melanocytes.
Risks and caveats: Intravenous use outside medical indications has been linked to rashes and severe allergic or skin reactions, and some regulators, including the Philippine FDA and dermatology societies, have issued warnings. Injectable products from informal sources carry contamination and dosing risks. Any lightening seen in small studies has been reported as mild and may reverse after stopping.
deepLead:
Glutathione (GSH) is a tripeptide built from glutamate, cysteine and glycine. It is the most abundant low-molecular-weight thiol in most cell types and acts as an antioxidant, protecting cellular components from reactive oxygen species, peroxides and heavy metals, and it takes part in the detoxification of drugs and other xenobiotics .
Outside its biochemistry, glutathione is sold as an oral, sublingual, topical and intravenous product, and it is marketed in parts of Asia and elsewhere for skin lightening. The proposed mechanisms include inhibition of tyrosinase, the key enzyme in melanin production, and a shift of melanin synthesis toward lighter pheomelanin . The same use is discussed on looksmaxxing forums .
A 2025 systematic review reported that several randomized trials of oral glutathione found a reduction in a skin melanin index compared with placebo, while noting that evidence for intravenous use is sparse . A separate 6-month trial examined whether oral glutathione raises body stores of the molecule . Professional bodies and regulators in some countries have issued warnings about intravenous use for lightening, as described below.

name: L-Cysteine

angle.text: L-cysteine is discussed as a glutathione precursor that might lighten skin, and also as a building block for hair keratin. It is also used by steroid users for general support. The lightening idea comes from pigment biochemistry and has little direct human evidence for cosmetic use.

summary: Antioxidant precursor tied to melanin pathways; weak lightening evidence.
currentQuick:
L-cysteine is a sulfur-containing amino acid that the body can make from methionine and that is also supplied by protein-rich foods. It is sold as a supplement and used in food processing, and its acetylated form N-acetylcysteine is a well-known medicine.
In skin-tone discussions it is mentioned as a glutathione precursor and because cysteine participates in melanin pathways. Evidence that it lightens skin is limited and mostly indirect.
How it works: Cysteine is the rate-limiting amino acid for glutathione synthesis. Its availability is also thought to steer melanocytes toward pheomelanin, the lighter pigment, rather than eumelanin. Whether supplemental doses meaningfully change visible pigmentation in people is unproven.
Risks and caveats: Typical dietary and low-dose supplemental intake is generally tolerated, with possible gastrointestinal upset. High doses can cause nausea and other effects, and people with cystinuria or on certain medications are advised to seek medical advice before use. Products marketed for lightening are not approved for that use.
deepLead:
Cysteine is a semiessential proteinogenic amino acid whose side chain carries a thiol (sulfhydryl) group. The L-form is a building block of proteins in all organisms; the thiol lets cysteine residues form disulfide bonds that stabilize protein structure, as in keratin, and bind metal ions . Humans can usually make it from methionine through the transsulfuration pathway, and it is also supplied by foods such as poultry, eggs, beef and whole grains .
In appearance-related discussion, L-cysteine comes up mainly as a precursor of glutathione, the cell's principal thiol antioxidant, and because cysteine availability is proposed to influence which melanin type is made in skin. It is sold as a supplement, appears in hair supplements, and has industrial uses in food processing and in permanent-wave hair treatments . Its acetylated derivative, N-acetylcysteine (NAC), is a long-established medicine used as a mucolytic and as an antidote to paracetamol poisoning .
No published human trial in the reference material tests supplemental L-cysteine itself for skin lightening or other cosmetic outcomes. Evidence for a pigment effect is indirect, drawn from biochemistry and from studies of related compounds.

name: Tretinoin

angle.text: Tretinoin is the most widely discussed prescription cream in skincare and looksmaxxing circles, used for acne, fine wrinkles, texture and uneven pigment. Its use for acne and photoaging is supported by decades of clinical trials. Early purging and irritation are commonly reported, and users debate how to tolerate them.

summary: The gold-standard retinoid: builds collagen, smooths fine wrinkles, clears acne, reverses photoaging.
currentQuick:
Tretinoin is all-trans retinoic acid, the biologically active form of vitamin A, and is sold as a prescription topical cream, gel or lotion under brands such as Retin-A. It was first developed for acne and later became the best-documented topical treatment for photoaged skin, where it is used to soften fine lines, even out pigmentation and improve texture.
In appearance-focused communities it is widely described as the benchmark anti-aging and acne ingredient. Clinical evidence includes long-term vehicle-controlled trials and systematic reviews, although many trials are small and use differing formulations and outcome measures.
How it works: Tretinoin binds nuclear retinoic acid receptors (RARs) and retinoid X receptors in skin cells and changes gene expression. This speeds up keratinocyte turnover, normalizes follicular keratinization so pores clog less, and reduces inflammation. In dermal fibroblasts it increases collagen synthesis and reduces the activity of matrix metalloproteinases that break collagen down, which underlies the improvements seen in photodamage. Because it is already the active acid, it does not need conversion in the skin, unlike retinol.
Risks and caveats: Irritation (redness, dryness, peeling, stinging) is common, particularly in the first weeks, and increased sun sensitivity is reported, so daily sun protection is advised. Topical retinoids are generally avoided in pregnancy because of the known teratogenic risk of systemic retinoids, even though systemic absorption from topical use is low. It is prescription-only in most countries. Results build slowly over months and fade if use stops.
deepLead:
Tretinoin is all-trans retinoic acid, the biologically active acid form of vitamin A. Applied to the skin as a prescription cream, gel or lotion (brand names include Retin-A), it is used for acne and for photoaged skin, where it is used to smooth fine wrinkles, roughness and uneven pigmentation. Taken by mouth in capsules, the same molecule is a cancer drug used to induce remission in acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) .
Its evidence base for skin is among the largest of any topical cosmetic drug. A 1988 double-blind, vehicle-controlled study in JAMA reported improvement of photoaged skin, a 1993 New England Journal of Medicine study reported restored collagen formation in photodamaged skin, and a 2022 systematic review examined the randomized trials of topical tretinoin for photoaging . Current US acne guidelines make a strong recommendation for topical retinoids as a class .
In skincare and looksmaxxing communities it is frequently described as the benchmark anti-aging and acne ingredient, and community discussion centres on obtaining it, tolerating the early irritation phase, and comparing it with over-the-counter retinol and adapalene . Documented adverse effects include irritation and sun sensitivity, and retinoids are associated with a teratogenic risk when taken systemically .

name: Retinol

chain: Converts to retinoic acid in skin
angle.text: Retinol is the over-the-counter vitamin A cosmetic, used as a milder alternative to tretinoin for fine lines, texture, acne marks and uneven tone, sometimes around the eyes. Trials support modest anti-aging effects on the face. Under-eye claims about filling dark circles are less studied.

summary: OTC vitamin-A derivative; converts to retinoic acid in skin.
note: Weaker than tretinoin but no prescription needed.
currentQuick:
Retinol is a form of vitamin A (an alcohol) used in over-the-counter serums and creams for fine lines, uneven tone and rough texture. It is one of the most common anti-aging cosmetic ingredients and is often positioned as a gentler step toward prescription retinoids.
Evidence for improvement in photoaged skin exists in clinical studies and reviews, but results are generally slower and milder than with tretinoin, and product concentration, formulation stability and packaging heavily influence real-world performance.
How it works: After it enters the skin, retinol is oxidized in two enzymatic steps to retinaldehyde and then to retinoic acid, which activates retinoic acid receptors and alters gene expression. The downstream effects are increased epidermal turnover, greater collagen production and less breakdown of existing collagen. Because conversion is limited and inefficient, the amount of retinoic acid generated is small, which explains both its milder effect and its better tolerability.
Risks and caveats: Dryness, redness, flaking and photosensitivity are the usual side effects and tend to ease with gradual introduction and moisturizer. Retinol is oxidation- and light-sensitive, so poorly formulated products may lose potency. Dermatology guidance generally advises avoiding topical retinoids during pregnancy as a precaution. It is sold without prescription but concentrations are regulated in some regions.
deepLead:
Retinol is the alcohol form of vitamin A (vitamin A1), a fat-soluble vitamin found in fish, dairy and meat and needed for vision, cell differentiation, skin and mucous-membrane maintenance, immune function and reproductive development. It is used as a supplement to treat and prevent vitamin A deficiency and, applied to the skin, as one of the most common over-the-counter anti-aging cosmetic ingredients .
In skin, retinol is converted in steps to retinal and then to retinoic acid, the active molecule that acts on nuclear retinoic acid receptors. Because the conversion is limited, retinol is generally described as milder than prescription tretinoin, which is retinoic acid itself . A review in the Journal of Drugs in Dermatology states that retinol has been shown to improve fine lines, wrinkles, hyperpigmentation, roughness and the look of photoaged skin, and that its tolerability makes it preferable for patients who cannot tolerate prescription retinoids .
Clinical evidence exists but is smaller than for tretinoin: a randomized vehicle-controlled study in elderly adults, a randomized comparison with the plant extract bakuchiol, and a systematic review of antiaging cosmeceuticals are among the main sources . Common adverse effects are dryness, redness, flaking and photosensitivity, and high-dose vitamin A during pregnancy may harm a fetus .

name: Adapalene

angle.text: Adapalene gel is the retinoid sold without a prescription in the US, used for acne on the face, back and shoulders, including testosterone-related breakouts, and for texture. Its acne benefit is established in trials. Use for aging is less studied, and claims that it outperforms tretinoin are not well supported.

summary: OTC retinoid for acne and texture — the strongest retinoid you can buy without a script.
currentQuick:
Adapalene is a synthetic third-generation topical retinoid developed for acne vulgaris. It became the first retinoid sold over the counter for acne in the United States in 2016 (as a 0.1% gel), following earlier prescription availability, and is also marketed in combination with benzoyl peroxide or clindamycin.
Beyond acne it is used off-label for texture, keratosis pilaris and some signs of photoaging. Many users describe it as the most accessible retinoid, since it can be bought without a prescription and is reported to cause less irritation than tretinoin.
How it works: Adapalene selectively activates retinoic acid receptors beta and gamma, which normalizes follicular keratinocyte differentiation, prevents microcomedone formation and has direct anti-inflammatory effects. It is chemically more stable than tretinoin and less affected by light and benzoyl peroxide, which makes it easy to combine with other acne actives.
Risks and caveats: Initial dryness, redness, burning and peeling are common and typically peak in the first few weeks. Photosensitivity is reported, and daily sunscreen is generally advised. Use in pregnancy is generally discouraged despite reassuring limited human data. Benefits take about 8 to 12 weeks to appear, and combining with other irritants can worsen tolerability.
deepLead:
Adapalene, sold under the brand name Differin among others, is a third-generation synthetic topical retinoid used mainly for mild to moderate acne vulgaris. It is used off-label for keratosis pilaris and has been explored for photoaging and other conditions . Since 2016 a 0.1 percent adapalene gel has been available over the counter in the United States, the first formerly prescription-only retinoid to be sold that way for acne .
Guidelines list topical retinoids, with adapalene the principal example in UK guidance, as first-line acne treatment, either alone or with benzoyl peroxide or an antibiotic . A systematic review of 54 trials of US-approved topical retinoids found them superior to vehicle on investigator global assessments .
Wikipedia describes adapalene as often regarded as the best tolerated of the three topical retinoids, with less irritation than tretinoin, and as chemically more stable, so that it can be used with benzoyl peroxide and is less affected by light . Typical adverse effects are dryness, redness, burning and peeling in the first weeks, and photosensitivity .

name: Tazarotene

angle.text: Tazarotene is a prescription topical retinoid used for acne and photoaging, and forum users describe it as a more intense option than tretinoin. It is studied for acne, psoriasis and fine wrinkles. Reports of heavy peeling and sun sensitivity are common, and claims of a 'feminizing' glow are anecdotal.

summary: Potent topical retinoid for acne and photoaging.
currentQuick:
Tazarotene is a prescription acetylenic topical retinoid approved for acne vulgaris, plaque psoriasis and, in cream form, for facial fine wrinkling and pigment irregularities from sun damage. It is generally considered one of the most potent topical retinoids.
Its potency leads to its use in stubborn acne and photodamage, but irritation is a frequent limiting factor, so newer lotion and foam formulations and combinations with other agents have been developed.
How it works: Tazarotene is a prodrug converted in the skin to tazarotenic acid, which selectively binds retinoic acid receptors beta and gamma. This normalizes keratinocyte proliferation and differentiation, reduces inflammation and influences genes involved in skin repair, producing improvements in acne lesions, psoriatic plaques and photoaged skin.
Risks and caveats: Local irritation, dryness, peeling and photosensitivity are common. Tazarotene carries a boxed pregnancy warning in some labels because of teratogenicity concerns, and pregnancy testing and contraception are advised for people who could become pregnant. It requires a prescription.
deepLead:
Tazarotene, sold as Tazorac, Arazlo and other brands, is a third-generation acetylenic topical retinoid used for acne vulgaris and plaque psoriasis. Certain formulations are also used to reduce signs of photoaging such as fine facial wrinkles and mottled pigmentation. It is a prodrug converted in the skin to the active tazarotenic acid . It was approved for medical use in 1997 and is available as a generic .
It is generally regarded as a potent topical retinoid, and irritation is a recurring limiting factor, which has driven newer lotion and foam formulations and combination products . A 2024 US guideline strongly recommends topical retinoids as a class for acne .
Tazarotene is a known teratogen and is contraindicated in pregnancy; the US label requires a negative pregnancy test within two weeks before starting in people who could become pregnant, plus effective contraception . It is prescription-only.

name: Isotretinoin

angle.text: Isotretinoin is an oral retinoid prescribed for severe acne and used by people seeking a lasting clear complexion. Its effect on severe acne is well studied. Forum claims include hormonal or mood side effects and combining it with steroids or heavy training, which are discussed largely through anecdote and case reports.

summary: Systemic retinoid for severe, treatment-resistant acne.
currentQuick:
Isotretinoin (13-cis retinoic acid, formerly sold as Accutane) is an oral retinoid reserved for severe, scarring or treatment-resistant acne. It is described as the only acne therapy capable of producing long-lasting remission in many patients and is also used off-label for severe rosacea and some other conditions.
In looksmaxxing circles it is discussed as a treatment for severe acne, and its side-effect burden and regulatory controls mean it is used under medical supervision.
How it works: Isotretinoin markedly reduces the size of sebaceous glands and lowers sebum output, normalizes follicular keratinization, reduces growth of acne-associated bacteria indirectly by changing the follicular environment, and has anti-inflammatory effects. It likely acts partly through induction of cell death in sebocytes and changes in retinoid-responsive gene expression.
Risks and caveats: It is a potent teratogen and is distributed under strict risk-management programs (such as iPLEDGE in the US) requiring pregnancy prevention. Common effects include dry lips, skin and eyes; laboratory monitoring is needed for lipids and liver enzymes. Reports of mood changes have been studied extensively, and a recent meta-analysis found no clear increase in suicide risk, though monitoring remains standard. It is prescription-only.
deepLead:
Isotretinoin (13-cis-retinoic acid), sold under the brand name Accutane and others, is an oral retinoid related to vitamin A. It is approved for severe recalcitrant nodular acne, and dermatologists also use it for moderate acne that resists other treatment or causes scarring or psychological distress, as well as for conditions such as harlequin ichthyosis . The US label reserves it for severe nodular acne unresponsive to conventional therapy including systemic antibiotics .
The 2024 American Academy of Dermatology guideline strongly recommends oral isotretinoin for acne that is severe, that causes psychosocial burden or scarring, or that fails standard oral or topical therapy . Isotretinoin was patented in 1969 and approved for medical use in 1982 .
It is a potent teratogen carrying a boxed warning, and in the United States it is dispensed under the iPLEDGE risk-management program . Common effects are dry lips, skin and eyes and sun sensitivity, and the drug label also warns about psychiatric disorders . Reviews of prospective studies and meta-analyses describe the depression association as reassuring, while some adverse effects, such as sexual dysfunction reported to the UK regulator, have drawn regulatory notices . It is prescription-only.

name: Botulinum toxin A

angle.text: Botulinum toxin injections are used cosmetically to smooth forehead and eye-area lines and, off-label, to slim the jaw by relaxing the masseter or to reduce clenching. Wrinkle use is approved and well studied. Jaw slimming and facial symmetry uses are less studied, and concerns about a frozen look are commonly discussed.

summary: Relaxes facial muscles to erase dynamic wrinkles.
currentQuick:
Botulinum toxin type A is a purified neurotoxin injected in tiny amounts to weaken targeted muscles. Products such as onabotulinumtoxinA (Botox) are among the most common cosmetic procedures worldwide and are used to soften dynamic wrinkles such as frown lines, forehead lines and crow's feet.
Beyond wrinkle treatment, practitioners use it for masseter slimming, brow shaping and other contouring effects. It is also approved for numerous medical indications, including migraine and spasticity. Results are temporary and require repeat treatment.
How it works: The toxin enters motor nerve terminals and cleaves SNAP-25, a protein in the SNARE complex needed to release acetylcholine. Without acetylcholine release the injected muscle relaxes, and overlying skin creases soften because the muscle can no longer fold it. Effects last a few months until nerve terminals regenerate.
Risks and caveats: Typical effects are bruising, headache and temporary asymmetry or drooping of an eyelid or brow if the toxin spreads to unintended muscles. Rare systemic spread can cause serious weakness. Some patients develop reduced response over time, possibly linked to neutralizing antibodies. It is a prescription drug that is administered by trained clinicians; counterfeit products are a recognized hazard.
deepLead:
Botulinum toxin type A (BoNT-A) is a neurotoxic protein made by the bacterium Clostridium botulinum. It blocks release of the neurotransmitter acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, causing temporary flaccid paralysis of the injected muscle. In heavily diluted form it is used for medical and cosmetic purposes, and commercial products include Botox Cosmetic, Dysport, Xeomin, Jeuveau and Daxxify .
Cosmetically it is injected to soften dynamic wrinkles, especially in the upper third of the face: glabellar (frown) lines, forehead lines and crow's feet. Wikipedia describes it as considered relatively safe and effective for this, with an effect that is usually visible three to five days after injection and lasts typically two to four months for glabellar lines, in some patients up to six months or longer . Appearance-related uses discussed by clinicians also include masseter slimming and brow shaping .
Medical uses are broad, including chronic migraine, spasticity, dystonia, overactive bladder, hyperhidrosis and strabismus . Every botulinum toxin label carries a boxed warning about distant spread of toxin effect, and a meta-analysis of cosmetic upper-face injections reported an overall complication rate of 16 percent, with headache, local skin reactions and facial neuromuscular symptoms the most common .

name: Azelaic acid

angle.text: Azelaic acid is used in skincare for acne, redness and dark spots, and as a gentler alternative to hydroquinone for melasma. Those skin uses have clinical trial support. Its use as a scalp 'DHT inhibitor' for hair loss, sometimes mixed with minoxidil, is a forum claim with little human evidence.

summary: Triple threat: acne, redness, and dark spots in one ingredient.
currentQuick:
Azelaic acid is a naturally occurring dicarboxylic acid used topically for acne, rosacea and post-inflammatory or melasma-type hyperpigmentation. Prescription strengths of 15 to 20 percent exist, and lower-strength cosmetic versions are sold over the counter in many markets.
It is used for its breadth of action: a single ingredient addresses bumps, redness and dark marks, and it is generally acceptable in people who cannot tolerate retinoids.
How it works: Azelaic acid has antibacterial effects against acne-associated bacteria, normalizes follicular keratinization, suppresses inflammatory pathways and reactive oxygen species, and competitively inhibits tyrosinase in overactive melanocytes, which explains its use in hyperpigmentation.
Risks and caveats: Stinging, itching and dryness are the most common effects and usually fade with continued use. Systemic absorption is low and it is widely considered compatible with pregnancy, though individual advice should come from a clinician. Results take weeks to months.
deepLead:
Azelaic acid (nonanedioic acid) is a nine-carbon saturated dicarboxylic acid found naturally in grains such as wheat, rye and barley and produced on human skin by the yeast Malassezia furfur. Industrially it is made by ozonolysis of oleic acid and is used in polymers, plasticizers and lubricants, as well as in some hair and skin conditioners.
In dermatology it is applied topically for acne vulgaris, papulopustular rosacea and pigmentation disorders such as melasma and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. Prescription products typically contain 15 to 20 percent, and lower-strength cosmetic versions are sold over the counter in some markets. A US prescription gel (15 percent) is labelled for the inflammatory papules and pustules of mild to moderate rosacea. A 2024 American Academy of Dermatology acne guideline makes a conditional recommendation for azelaic acid, a weaker grade than the strong recommendations it gives for benzoyl peroxide and topical retinoids.
A 2025 Delphi consensus of 62 dermatologists listed azelaic acid among 23 ingredients that cosmetic dermatologists frequently recommend, for acne and for dark spots. In online communities it is discussed mainly as a skin-care ingredient for bumps, redness and marks, and, separately, as an ingredient in scalp products that proponents describe as anti-androgenic; the latter use has not been established in published clinical trials.

name: Niacinamide

angle.text: Niacinamide serums and creams are used for oil control, enlarged-looking pores, uneven tone and general skin quality. Trials have studied acne, pigmentation and aging in topical forms. Claims about anxiety, NAD+ energy and TRT symptoms come from oral supplement discussions and are mostly untested for appearance.

summary: Barrier support, oil control, and pigment evening.
currentQuick:
Niacinamide (nicotinamide) is the amide form of vitamin B3 and a staple ingredient in cosmetic serums and moisturizers. Typical claims include improved barrier function, reduced oil appearance and pore prominence, calmer redness and a more even tone.
Clinical studies support modest benefits for hyperpigmentation, barrier function and some inflammatory acne, but effect sizes are generally small and vary between formulations.
How it works: Niacinamide is a precursor of NAD+ and NADP+, coenzymes central to cellular energy and repair. In skin it increases ceramide and barrier lipid synthesis, reduces sebum output and interferes with the transfer of melanosomes from melanocytes to keratinocytes, helping to lighten uneven pigment.
Risks and caveats: It is generally very well tolerated. Occasional flushing, itching or irritation occurs, especially at higher concentrations or in poorly formulated products. It is sold freely as a cosmetic ingredient.
deepLead:
Niacinamide, also called nicotinamide, is the amide form of vitamin B3. It is found in foods such as yeast, meat, milk and green vegetables, is sold as a dietary supplement and medication, and is incorporated into cosmetic serums, moisturizers and cleansers. Within cells it is a precursor of the coenzymes NAD+ and NADP+, which take part in many oxidation-reduction reactions. Unlike nicotinic acid (niacin), it does not cause skin flushing at ordinary doses.
In skin care it is promoted for improving barrier function, reducing sebum, evening skin tone and calming redness. Reviews describe antipruritic, antimicrobial, vasoactive, photoprotective, sebostatic and lightening effects that depend on concentration and on how well the compound is delivered into skin. A 2025 Delphi consensus of 62 dermatologists included niacinamide among the ingredients cosmetic dermatologists frequently recommend, for redness and dark spots.
Published human trials are mostly small, often industry-linked, and use short treatment periods; one 2014 review noted that existing data were not sufficient for a scientifically founded evaluation of its therapeutic use even while describing the prospects as interesting. Outside cosmetics, oral nicotinamide is used to treat pellagra and has been studied for non-melanoma skin cancer prevention and glaucoma.

name: Vitamin C (topical)

angle.text: Topical vitamin C serums are used to brighten skin, fade dark spots and acne marks, and limit photoaging. Small trials support brightening and some wrinkle improvement. Stability of the formulation, and whether derivatives perform like ascorbic acid, are common forum debates.

summary: Antioxidant that brightens, fades spots, and supports collagen pathways.
currentQuick:
Topical vitamin C, most often as L-ascorbic acid, is used in serums intended to brighten the complexion, fade dark spots and provide antioxidant protection against environmental damage. It is among the best-known cosmeceuticals, popular alongside sunscreen in morning routines.
Studies suggest benefits for photoaging and hyperpigmentation, but trials are often small, sometimes industry-funded, and effectiveness is highly dependent on formulation, pH, concentration and stability.
How it works: Ascorbic acid neutralizes free radicals generated by ultraviolet exposure, is a required cofactor for enzymes that stabilize collagen, and inhibits tyrosinase to reduce melanin production. It also helps regenerate vitamin E in skin. Skin penetration requires an acidic, adequately concentrated formulation.
Risks and caveats: L-ascorbic acid oxidizes easily, turning serums yellow or brown and reducing potency. Stinging and irritation can occur, particularly with low-pH products. It is not regarded as a substitute for sunscreen and is sold over the counter.
deepLead:
Topical vitamin C refers to skin-care products containing L-ascorbic acid or one of its derivatives, applied to the skin rather than taken by mouth. Vitamin C is a water-soluble vitamin that humans must obtain from diet; it serves as a cofactor in collagen formation and acts as an antioxidant. In cosmetic and dermatological use it is promoted for brightening, fading dark spots and reducing signs of photoaging.
A narrative review in the Journal of Clinical and Aesthetic Dermatology describes several proposed actions: neutralizing reactive oxygen species produced by ultraviolet light, supporting enzymes that stabilize collagen, inhibiting tyrosinase to reduce melanin formation, and regenerating vitamin E. The same review notes that clinical trials are small and that evidence for topical formulations is limited.
Product performance is discussed in terms of formulation: L-ascorbic acid is unstable and poorly penetrating unless formulated at a low pH and an adequate concentration, while more stable derivatives have been reported not to raise skin ascorbic acid levels in at least one study. Topical vitamin C is sold over the counter as serums and creams and is often paired with sunscreen in morning routines.

name: Tranexamic acid

angle.text: Tranexamic acid, topical or oral, is used for stubborn melasma and dark marks after acne. It is an approved bleeding drug, so cosmetic use is off-label. Trials in melasma exist, mostly small, and users compare it to hydroquinone, while its use for under-eye darkness is much less studied.

summary: Melasma and stubborn hyperpigmentation fighter, topical or oral (oral = Rx).
currentQuick:
Tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic drug first used to control bleeding. In dermatology it has become a popular option for melasma and stubborn hyperpigmentation, applied topically, injected in clinics or taken by mouth.
The cosmetic use of oral tranexamic acid is off-label and prescription-only, while topical products are sold over the counter in many places. Studies show meaningful improvement in melasma but with heterogeneous designs and recurrence after stopping.
How it works: It blocks plasmin formation, and in skin this appears to reduce plasmin-driven stimulation of melanocytes and related inflammatory and vascular signalling, decreasing melanin production and the vascular component of melasma.
Risks and caveats: Topical use is usually well tolerated, with mild irritation. Oral tranexamic acid carries a risk of blood clots and is unsuitable for people with a history of thromboembolism or those on estrogen-containing contraception; gastrointestinal upset and menstrual changes are possible. Oral use requires medical screening and supervision.
deepLead:
Tranexamic acid (TXA) is a synthetic derivative of the amino acid lysine that acts as an antifibrinolytic: it reversibly binds lysine-binding sites on plasminogen, reducing conversion to plasmin and so slowing the breakdown of fibrin clots. It is used to prevent or treat bleeding in trauma, postpartum haemorrhage, surgery, tooth removal, nosebleeds and heavy menstrual bleeding, and it is on the WHO List of Essential Medicines.
In dermatology it has become a widely discussed option for melasma and other stubborn hyperpigmentation, used orally, topically, by injection or microneedling-assisted delivery. Oral TXA for melasma is off-label (it is not approved for that indication by the US FDA or India's regulator, according to a 2023 Indian expert consensus), while topical cosmetic products containing TXA are sold in many markets.
Reviews describe promising results in melasma but heterogeneous study designs, small samples, unknown optimal duration and frequent relapse after treatment stops. A systematic review of melasma treatments notes that systemic TXA had promising results but was linked to systemic side effects, and that combination therapies generally performed best. The systemic form carries a thrombosis warning on its drug label.
